explanation:
## The program

```cpp
int total{ a + b + c };

std::cout << "integer " << total / 3 << "\n";

double exact{ static_cast<double>(total) / 3 };
std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2);
std::cout << "exact " << exact << "\n";
```

## The conversion has to happen before the division

This is the single most common beginner arithmetic bug in C++, and
it is silent — nothing warns, and the answer is plausible.

```cpp
double a{ 7 / 3 };                          // 2.0
double b{ static_cast<double>(7) / 3 };     // 2.3333...
double c{ 7 / 3.0 };                        // 2.3333...
double d{ static_cast<double>(7 / 3) };     // 2.0  — too late
```

The rule is that `/` looks at the types of its two operands and
nothing else. Two `int`s means integer division; what the result is
assigned to is not part of that decision, so `a` and `d` have already
lost the fraction by the time the conversion happens. One `double`
operand is enough to make it a real division, which is why `b` and
`c` both work.

## Truncation towards zero, again

`-7 / 3` is -2, not -3. The quotient is cut towards zero rather than
rounded or floored, so a negative mean comes out *larger* than the
true value while a positive one comes out smaller. If what you want
is a rounded integer mean, say so: `static_cast<int>(std::lround(
exact))`, or for non-negative integers the old trick of
`(total + 1) / 3`. Do not expect `/` to round.

## std::fixed and std::setprecision are sticky

They are not arguments to one print; they change the stream and stay
changed:

```cpp
std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2);
std::cout << 1.5 << " " << 2.0 << "\n";    // 1.50 2.00
```

Which is convenient here and a nuisance in a longer program, where
something printing a plain number three functions later suddenly has
two decimal places. `std::setw` is the exception — it applies to the
next item only.

## What this does not check

Rounding at the halfway point. The mean of three integers is either
exact to two places or an endless 3 or 6, so no case here lands on a
tie like 2.005 where the two common rounding rules disagree. A
program printing money would have to decide that question on
purpose; this one never meets it.
